issues.description: The PersonService.savePerson method has inconsistent return types between template and solution usage: the template's PersonService.savePerson returns a Person (allowing controllers/resources to return the saved Person), but in the solution repository PersonService.savePerson is declared to return void while PersonResource (solution) calls personService.savePerson(...) and uses its return value as a Person. This mismatch makes the solution codebase internally inconsistent and would prevent compilation or confuse students about the intended API contract for saving a Person.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the PersonService.savePerson method signature consistent with how it is used by the REST resource and the template. Either change PersonService.savePerson to return Person (and return the saved/updated Person) so PersonResource can call ResponseEntity.ok(personService.savePerson(...)), or adjust PersonResource to not expect a return value (e.g., return the person passed in or fetch it after saving). Prefer restoring the savePerson(Person) -> Person signature (as in the template) to align with the REST contract described in the problem statement.

issues.description: The client-side controller uses the method name 'editNote' for the update action, while the server-side REST resource names the corresponding action 'updateNote'. Both refer to the same conceptual operation (updating a Note), but the differing identifiers between client and server create a minor mapping mismatch compared to the CRUD 'update' terminology used in the problem statement. This can cause brief cognitive overhead for students linking the client implementation to the server API and the stated requirements.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the identifier names for the update action: rename the client method 'editNote' to 'updateNote' (or rename the server method to 'editNote') so client and server use the same verb for the same conceptual operation. Update all call sites accordingly to keep naming consistent with the CRUD 'update' terminology in the problem statement.
